To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) the reward-related decision-making process is impaired in individuals with overweight/obesity compared with normal-weight controls, (b) this impairment was related to the degree of overweight, and (c) the reward-related deficit in decision making was related to weight loss maintenance in individuals with overweight and obesity.

(a) the ability to make reward-related decisions, as measured by the Iowa Gambling Task (IGT), is associated with long-term weight loss, (b) the ability to use reward-related information to guide decisions, as measured in the IGT, is associated with weight loss maintenance, and (c) the ability to learn from reward-related decision making, as measured in a novel task that was developed to assess learning from reward-related decision-making, is associated with short-term weight loss.

The findings of our study suggest that individuals with a higher BMI are less likely to engage in reward-based decision making, and that the ability to engage in reward-related decision making is a predictor of weight loss maintenance in the short-term and long-term, but not weight loss in the short-term.
